🔑 MASTER FORMULA & KEY-FACTS SHEET (keep for revision)

Unit 1 (Sets):

  • Number of subsets of a set with n elements = 2ⁿ; proper subsets = 2ⁿ − 1.
  • Union: A ∪ B = {x : x∈A or x∈B}. Intersection: A ∩ B = {x : x∈A and x∈B}.
  • Disjoint sets: A ∩ B = ∅.
  • Complement: A′ = {x : x∈U and x∉A}.
  • Difference: A − B = A \ B = A ∩ B′.
  • Symmetric difference: A Δ B = (A\B) ∪ (B\A) = (A∪B) \ (A∩B).
  • De Morgan's laws: (A∪B)′ = A′∩B′ and (A∩B)′ = A′∪B′.
  • n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B).
  • Cartesian product: A×B = {(a,b) : a∈A, b∈B}.

Unit 2 (Number System):

  • Euclid's division lemma: a = bq + r, 0 ≤ r < b.
  • Prime: exactly 2 factors. Composite: > 2 factors. 1 is neither; 2 is the only even prime.
  • Divisibility: 2 (unit digit even), 3 & 9 (sum of digits divisible), 4 (last 2 digits), 5 (ends 0/5), 6 (÷2 and ÷3), 8 (last 3 digits), 10 (ends 0).
  • Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite = unique product of primes.
  • GCF × LCM = a × b (for two numbers).
  • Rational ℚ = {a/b : a,b∈ℤ, b≠0}; terminating or repeating decimals.
  • Irrational: non-terminating, non-repeating (e.g., √2, π).
  • ℝ = ℚ ∪ irrationals. If a<b then √a < √b (a,b>0).
  • Radicals: √a·√b = √(ab); √a/√b = √(a/b); a√b = √(a²b); √(a²b) = a√b.
  • Laws of exponents: aⁿaᵐ=aⁿ⁺ᵐ; aⁿ/aᵐ=aⁿ⁻ᵐ; (aⁿ)ᵐ=aⁿᵐ; (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ; (a/b)ⁿ=aⁿ/bⁿ; a⁰=1; a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ.
  • Absolute value |x| = x if x≥0, −x if x<0.
  • Scientific notation: a×10ⁿ with 1≤a<10.
  • Upper/lower bound: value ± (place value ÷ 2).
  • Intervals: [a,b] closed; (a,b) open; [a,b) half-open.

Unit 3 (Equations):

  • Linear (1 var): ax + b = 0, a≠0, one solution.
  • Linear (2 vars): ax + by = c.
  • System solutions: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ → infinite (coincident); a₁/a₂=b₁/b₂≠c₁/c₂ → none (parallel); a₁/a₂≠b₁/b₂ → one (intersect).
  • Methods: table, substitution, elimination, graphical.
  • |x| = p → x = p or x = −p (p≥0). |x| = −p → no solution.
  • Quadratic: ax²+bx+c=0 (a≠0). Solve by factorization, completing the square, or quadratic formula.
  • Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / (2a).
  • Discriminant D = b²−4ac: D>0 two real roots; D=0 one real root; D<0 no real roots.
  • Sum of roots = −b/a; product = c/a.
  • For a>0, aˣ = aʸ iff x=y.
  • Radical equations: isolate radical, square/raise both sides, check domain, verify.

Unit 4 (Inequalities):

  • Adding/subtracting same value: sign unchanged.
  • Multiply/divide by positive: sign unchanged; by negative: sign reverses.
  • Intervals on number line: open dot = excluded, closed dot = included.
  • |x| < a → −a < x < a; |x| > a → x < −a or x > a.
  • Two-variable inequalities: shade one side of boundary line (solid if ≤/≥, dashed if </>).
  • Product rule: m·n>0 if (m>0,n>0) or (m<0,n<0); m·n<0 if opposite signs.
  • Quadratic inequalities: solve by product property, sign chart, or graph.

Unit 5 (Trigonometry):

  • Pythagoras: b² + p² = h².
  • sin A = opposite/hypotenuse; cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse; tan A = opposite/adjacent.
  • tan A = sin A / cos A.
  • Basic values:
Anglesincostan
0°010
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/21/2√3
90°10undefined
  • sin A = cos(90° − A).

Unit 6 (Regular Polygons):

  • Sum of interior angles of n-gon = (n−2)×180°.
  • Sum of exterior angles = 360° (any polygon).
  • Each interior angle of regular n-gon = (n−2)×180°/n.
  • Each exterior angle = 360°/n. Each central angle = 360°/n.
  • Regular n-gon has n lines of symmetry.
  • Inscribed polygon formulas (radius r): s = 2r sin(180°/n); a = r cos(180°/n); P = 2nr sin(180°/n); A = ½ aP.

Unit 7 (Congruency & Similarity):

  • Congruent: same size AND shape (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS).
  • Similar: same shape, proportional sides, equal angles (AA, SSS, SAS similarity).
  • Ratio of perimeters of similar figures = ratio of corresponding sides.
  • Ratio of areas of similar figures = (ratio of sides)².

Unit 8 (Vectors):

  • Scalar: magnitude only. Vector: magnitude + direction.
  • Column vector ā = (x, y); magnitude |ā| = √(x²+y²).
  • Equality: same magnitude & direction. Opposite: −ā.
  • Parallel: one is scalar multiple of other.
  • Triangle law: AB + BC = AC. Parallelogram law: diagonal = sum of side vectors.
  • (p,q)+(r,s) = (p+r, q+s); subtraction subtracts components.
  • k(x,y) = (kx, ky). Position vector: (x₂−x₁, y₂−y₁).

Unit 9 (Statistics & Probability):

  • Mean x̄ = Σx/n = Σfx/Σf.
  • Median: middle value (average of two middles for even n).
  • Mode: most frequent value.
  • Range = largest − smallest.
  • Variance σ² = Σ(x−x̄)²/n. Standard deviation σ = √variance.
  • Adding constant k to data: variance unchanged. Multiplying by c: new variance = c²·(old), new σ = |c|·(old).
  • Probability P(E) = n(E)/n(S).
  • Sample space = all possible outcomes; event = subset of sample space.

🎯 TOP 15 EXAM TRAPS (quick scan)

  1. 2ⁿ vs 2ⁿ−1 — subsets vs proper subsets (proper excludes the set itself).
  2. 1 is neither prime nor composite — don't classify it.
  3. Multiplying/dividing an inequality by a negative reverses the sign — the #1 inequality error.
  4. |x| = negative → no solution — absolute value can never be negative.
  5. √(a²b) = a√b only when a>0 — watch signs.
  6. Discriminant D = b²−4ac — D>0 two distinct roots, D=0 one, D<0 none (real).
  7. Graph shading — solid line for ≤/≥, dashed for </>; test point (0,0) unless on the line.
  8. Sum of exterior angles is always 360° regardless of side count.
  9. Area ratio = (side ratio)², not the side ratio itself.
  10. Median: sort data first! Never find the middle of unsorted data.
  11. Even number of data → median is the average of the two middle values.
  12. Standard deviation changes when data are multiplied/divided but not when added/subtracted.
  13. Vectors: equality needs same magnitude AND direction; parallel just needs same/opposite direction.
  14. Complement A′ is with respect to U — always state the universal set.
  15. For a system, check whether lines are coincident/parallel/intersecting using the ratios of coefficients before solving.

📖 GLOSSARY OF KEY TERMS (quick definitions for revision)

Absolute value – the distance of a number from 0 on the number line; |x| = x if x≥0, −x if x<0.

Apothem – the perpendicular segment from the center of a regular polygon to the midpoint of a side.

Average (mean) – the sum of all values divided by the number of values.

Bar graph/chart – a graph using vertical or horizontal bars to represent data.

Base (exponent) – the number being raised to a power in an exponential expression.

Boundary line – the line that separates the solution region of a two-variable inequality from the rest of the plane.

Cardinality / number of elements – n(A) is the number of elements of set A.

Cartesian product – A×B = {(a,b): a∈A and b∈B}, the set of all ordered pairs.

Census – a complete enumeration of a population.

Central angle – the angle at the center of a circle formed by two radii to adjacent vertices of an inscribed polygon.

Circumcircle – the circle passing through all vertices of a polygon (polygon is inscribed in it).

Closed interval – [a,b], includes endpoints a and b.

Column vector – a vector written as a vertical pair (x, y).

Common factor – a number that is a factor of two or more given numbers.

Complement – A′ = all elements of U not in A.

Composite number – a natural number with more than two factors.

Concave polygon – a polygon with at least one interior angle > 180°.

Congruent triangles – triangles with the same three sides and same three angles.

Continuous data – data that can be measured at any value along a scale.

Convex polygon – a polygon where every interior angle < 180°.

Cosine – adjacent ÷ hypotenuse (cos A).

Decagon – a ten-sided polygon.

De Morgan's laws – (A∪B)′ = A′∩B′ and (A∩B)′ = A′∪B′.

Dependent system – a linear system with infinitely many solutions (coincident lines).

Difference of sets – A−B = {x: x∈A and x∉B}.

Discrete data – data that are counted (usually integers).

Discriminant – D = b²−4ac, determines the number of real roots of a quadratic.

Disjoint sets – sets with no common elements (A∩B = ∅).

Divisibility test – a rule to check divisibility without performing division.

Empty (null/void) set – a set with no elements, denoted ∅ or { }.

Equal sets – sets with exactly the same elements.

Equivalent sets – sets with the same number of elements (one-to-one correspondence).

Euclid's division lemma – for a≥0, b>0, there exist unique q,r with a = bq + r, 0≤r<b.

Event – a subset of a sample space.

Exterior angle – the angle formed outside a polygon by a side and the extension of an adjacent side.

Factor – a number that divides another number exactly.

Finite set – a set with a definite number of elements.

Frequency – the number of times a value occurs in a data set.

Frequency distribution – a table showing each value and its frequency.

GCF/HCF – the greatest (highest) common factor of two or more numbers.

Histogram – a bar graph of a frequency distribution (variable on x-axis, frequency on y-axis).

Hypotenuse – the side opposite the right angle; the longest side of a right triangle.

Incircle – the circle inside a polygon that touches each side at its midpoint.

Inconsistent system – a linear system with no solution (parallel lines).

Infinite set – a set that is not finite.

Interior angle – an angle formed inside a polygon.

Intersection – A∩B = elements common to both A and B.

Irrational number – a decimal that is neither terminating nor repeating (e.g., √2, π).

LCM – the least common multiple of two or more numbers.

Linear equation (1 var) – ax + b = 0, a≠0.

Linear equation (2 vars) – ax + by = c.

Line of symmetry – the line through which two halves of a figure match exactly.

Mean – x̄ = Σx/n.

Median – the middle value of ordered data.

Mode – the most frequent value.

nth root – √ⁿb; the number whose nth power is b.

Open interval – (a,b), excludes endpoints.

Opposite vector – same magnitude, opposite direction (−ā).

Parallel vectors – vectors with the same or opposite direction.

Perfect square – a number that is the square of an integer.

Pie chart – a circle divided into sectors proportional to the frequencies.

Polygon – a simple closed plane figure made of three or more line segments.

Population – the complete collection of individuals/objects under study.

Position vector – a vector that starts at the origin; (x₂−x₁, y₂−y₁).

Prime factorization – expressing a composite number as a product of primes.

Prime number – a natural number with exactly two factors (1 and itself).

Principal nth root – the positive nth root of a positive number.

Probability – P(E) = n(E)/n(S); the likelihood of an event.

Proper subset – A⊂B if A⊆B and A≠B.

Quadratic equation – ax²+bx+c=0, a≠0.

Quadratic formula – x = (−b±√(b²−4ac))/2a.

Qualitative data – data describing non-numerical characteristics (colour, sex, religion).

Quantitative data – numerical data (scores, heights, weights).

Radical – an expression with a root symbol √; √ⁿb has index n and radicand b.

Rationalizing – removing a radical from the denominator using the rationalizing factor.

Rational number – any number of form a/b, a,b∈ℤ, b≠0.

Range – largest value − smallest value.

Real number – a rational or irrational number.

Repeating decimal – a decimal with a repeating block of digits.

Sample – a subset of a population studied to draw conclusions.

Sample space – the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.

Scale factor – the ratio of corresponding sides of similar/enlarged figures.

Scalar – a quantity described by magnitude only.

Scalar multiple – kā, a vector k times the magnitude of ā.

Scientific notation – a×10ⁿ with 1≤a<10.

Set – a collection of well-defined distinct objects.

Set-builder notation – {x : property}.

Sign chart – a chart showing the sign of a factorized expression in each interval.

Significant figures – the meaningful digits of a number.

Similar figures – figures with congruent corresponding angles and proportional sides.

Sine – opposite ÷ hypotenuse (sin A).

Standard deviation – the square root of the variance.

Subset – A⊆B if every element of A is also in B.

Symmetric difference – AΔB = (A\B)∪(B\A).

Tangent – opposite ÷ adjacent (tan A).

Terminating decimal – a decimal that ends after a finite number of digits.

Tree diagram – a diagram showing all possible outcomes of a repeated experiment.

Universal set (U) – the set containing all elements of related sets.

Variance – the mean of the squared deviations from the mean.

Vector – a quantity with both magnitude and direction.

Venn diagram – a diagram representing sets as interlocking circles within a rectangle (U).

Zero vector – a vector with no magnitude and no direction.

UNIT 1: FURTHER ON SETS

Note: Based on the official FDRE MoE Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook (New Curriculum, 2023), Unit 1.

1.1 Sets and Elements

A set is a collection of well-defined objects or elements. "Well-defined" means that given any object, we can decide whether it belongs to the set or not.

  • If a is an element of set A, we write a ∈ A ("a belongs to A").
  • If b is not an element of A, we write b ∉ A ("b does not belong to A").
  • Sets are usually named with capital letters (A, B, X, …); elements with small letters (a, b, x, …).

Examples:

  • The set of students in your class is a well-defined set (members are clearly known).
  • "The collection of kind students in your school" is not well-defined — it is hard to decide who is "kind."
  • If G = {vowel letters}, then a ∈ G, o ∈ G, but b ∉ G.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: A set must be well-defined — you must be able to tell whether any given object is in the set or not. Examples that are NOT well-defined: "beautiful girls," "hardworking teachers," "kind students."

Example: If A = set of positive even numbers {2, 4, 6, 8, …}, then 4 ∈ A, 5 ∉ A, −2 ∉ A, 0 ∉ A.

1.2 Set Description

Sets can be described in three (or four) ways:

i) Verbal (statement) method — describe the elements in words.

  • Example: "The set of whole numbers greater than 1 and less than 20."

ii) Listing methods:

  • Complete listing (roster) method — list ALL elements in braces { }.
  • {2, 4, 6} = even positive integers less than 7.
  • {a, e, i, o, u} = vowels.
  • Partial listing method — list a few elements and use "…" when full listing is impossible.
  • {1, 2, 3, …, 99} = natural numbers less than 100.
  • 𝕎 = {0, 1, 2, 3, …} = whole numbers.

iii) Set-builder method (defining property) — {x : condition on x}.

  • A = {1, 2, …, 10} = {x : x ∈ ℕ and x < 11}.
  • B = {0, 2, 4, …} = {x : x ∈ ℤ and x is a non-negative even integer} = {2x : x ∈ 𝕎}.

Number sets you must know:

  • ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …} (natural numbers)
  • 𝕎 = {0, 1, 2, 3, …} (whole numbers)
  • ℤ = {…, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …} (integers)
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Know the three methods of describing a set (verbal, listing/roster, set-builder) and the symbols ℕ, 𝕎, ℤ.

1.3 The Notion of Sets

Empty, finite, and infinite sets

  • Empty (null/void) set: contains no element; denoted { } or ∅.
  • A = {x : 1 < x < 2, x ∈ ℕ} is empty (no natural number between 1 and 2).
  • Finite set: has a definite number of elements.
  • Infinite set: not finite.

Equal, equivalent, universal, subset, proper subset

  • Equal sets (A = B): exactly the same elements. {1,2,3,4} = {4,3,2,1}.
  • Equivalent sets (A↔B or A~B): one-to-one correspondence, so n(A) = n(B). {1,2,3,4} and {Red,Blue,Green,Black} are equivalent (4 each).
  • Universal set (U): contains all related elements without repetition.
  • Subset (A ⊆ B): every element of A is in B.

(A ⊆ B means the set A lies entirely inside B — every element of A is also in B.)

  • Proper subset (A ⊂ B): A ⊆ B and A ≠ B.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know — counting subsets:
Note: - Number of subsets of a set with n elements = 2ⁿ.
Note: - Number of proper subsets = 2ⁿ − 1.
Note: - Example: A = {1,2,3} has 2³ = 8 subsets and 7 proper subsets.
Note: - Any set is a subset of itself; the empty set is a subset of every set; ∅ is a proper subset of every non-empty set.

Example: For A = {2, 5, 7} and B = {2, 5, 7, 8}, A is a proper subset of B: A ⊂ B. Also B ⊄ A.

1.4 Operations on Sets

A Venn diagram represents sets as interlocking circles enclosed in a rectangle (the universal set U).

Union and Intersection

  • Union (A ∪ B) = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B} — everything in A or B (or both).
  • Intersection (A ∩ B) = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B} — elements common to both.
  • Two sets are disjoint if A ∩ B = ∅.
Union of two sets
Intersection of two sets

Example: U = natural numbers < 12, A = {1,2,3,4,5,6}, B = {1,3,5,7,9}.

  • A ∪ B = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,9}
  • A ∩ B = {1,3,5}

Complement

  • Complement of A (A′) = {x : x ∈ U and x ∉ A} — everything in U not in A.
Complement of a set

Example: U = {0,1,2,3,4}, A = {3,4} → A′ = {0,1,2}.

Difference of sets

  • A − B (or A \ B) = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B} — elements of A not in B. This is the relative complement of A w.r.t. B.
Difference of two sets

Example: A = {0,1,2,3,4}, B = {3,4} → A − B = {0,1,2}.

Key identities (Theorem 1.1):

  • (A′)' = A
  • A′ = U − A
  • A − B = A ∩ B′
  • A ⊆ B ⟺ B′ ⊆ A′

Symmetric Difference

  • A Δ B = (A \ B) ∪ (B \ A) = (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B).
Symmetric difference

Example: A = {1,2,4,5,8}, B = {2,3,5,7}. Then A\B = {1,4,8}, B\A = {3,7}, so AΔB = {1,3,4,7,8}.

Cartesian Product

  • A × B = {(a,b) : a ∈ A and b ∈ B} — the set of all ordered pairs.

Example: A = {1,2}, B = {a,b} → A×B = {(1,a),(1,b),(2,a),(2,b)}.

  • If A×B = {(1,a),(1,b),(2,a),(2,b),(3,a),(3,b)}, then A = {1,2,3}, B = {a,b}.
  • n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B).
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know — De Morgan's Laws:
Note: - 1st: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′
Note: - 2nd: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′
Note: These are extremely common in exams. Also know A − B = A ∩ B′.

1.5 Applications

Number of elements of a union

n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

  • If A ∩ B = ∅, then n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B).

Example: n(A) = 20, n(B) = 28, n(A∪B) = 36 → n(A∩B) = 20 + 28 − 36 = 12.

Worked application: In a meeting of 60 people, 42 drink tea and 27 drink coffee; everyone drinks at least one. Let T = tea-drinkers, C = coffee-drinkers.

  • n(T∪C) = 60 = n(T) + n(C) − n(T∩C) = 42 + 27 − n(T∩C) → n(T∩C) = 9 people drink both.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: For two sets, n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B). Use a Venn diagram for word problems about "how many do X only / both / neither."

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 1)

  • Set = well-defined collection of objects.
  • Describe sets by: verbal, roster (complete/partial listing), set-builder.
  • Empty set ∅; finite vs infinite; equal vs equivalent; universal set.
  • Subset ⊆, proper subset ⊂; number of subsets = 2ⁿ, proper = 2ⁿ−1.
  • Union ∪, intersection ∩, complement ′, difference − , symmetric difference Δ, product ×.
  • De Morgan: (A∪B)′ = A′∩B′; (A∩B)′ = A′∪B′.
  • n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B).
  • Venn diagrams are drawn as circles inside rectangle U.

UNIT 2: THE NUMBER SYSTEM

Note: Based on the official FDRE MoE Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook (New Curriculum, 2023), Unit 2.

2.1 Revision on Natural Numbers and Integers

  • Natural numbers ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}
  • Integers ℤ = {…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …}

Every natural number is an integer, but not every integer is a natural number (e.g., −7 and 0 are integers but not natural).

2.1.1 Euclid's Division Lemma

Theorem: Given a non-negative integer a and a positive integer b, there exist unique non-negative integers q (quotient) and r (remainder) such that:

a = b × q + r, with 0 ≤ r < b

  • a = dividend, b = divisor, q = quotient, r = remainder.
  • If r = 0, then a is divisible by b.

Examples:

  • 38 ÷ 4 → 38 = 4×9 + 2 (q=9, r=2).
  • 5 ÷ 14 → 5 = 14×0 + 5 (q=0, r=5).
  • 12 ÷ 3 → 12 = 3×4 + 0 (q=4, r=0).
  • 2574 ÷ 8 → 2574 = 8×321 + 6 (q=321, r=6).
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: a = bq + r with 0 ≤ r < b. The remainder is always less than the divisor. If r = 0, a is divisible by b.

2.1.2 Prime and Composite Numbers

  • Prime number: exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself). E.g., 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 53.
  • Composite number: more than two factors. E.g., 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 18.
  • 1 is neither prime nor composite.
  • 2 is the only even prime.
  • Factors of a number are always ≤ the number.

Example: 18 = 1×18 = 2×9 = 3×6, so 18 is composite. 53 = 1×53 only, so 53 is prime.

2.1.3 Divisibility Test

A number is divisible by:

  • 2 if its unit (last) digit is divisible by 2 (even).
  • 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
  • 4 if the number formed by its last two digits is divisible by 4.
  • 5 if its unit digit is 0 or 5.
  • 6 if it is divisible by both 2 and 3.
  • 8 if the number formed by its last three digits is divisible by 8.
  • 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.
  • 10 if its unit digit is 0.

Example: 2,334: divisible by 2 (unit digit 4 even), by 3 (sum 12), by 6 (÷2 and ÷3); NOT divisible by 4 (34 not ÷4), 5, 8, 9 (sum 12), or 10.

Prime Factorization & Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic

  • Prime factorization: expressing a composite number as a product of primes.
  • Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number can be factored into primes in a unique way (apart from order).

Examples:

  • 6 = 2×3
  • 30 = 2×3×5
  • 72 = 2³×3²
  • 456 = 2³×3×19 (456÷2=228, ÷2=114, ÷2=57, ÷3=19)

2.1.4 GCF and LCM

  • Common factor: a factor of each of several numbers.
  • GCF / HCF: the greatest common factor. Use prime factorization and take common primes with the least power.
  • LCM: the least common multiple. Take each prime with its highest power.
  • GCF × LCM = a × b for two numbers a, b.

Examples:

  • GCF(36, 56): 36 = 2²·3², 56 = 2³·7 → common prime 2 with least power 2² → GCF = 4.
  • GCF(12, 18, 36): 12=2²·3, 18=2·3², 36=2²·3² → GCF = 2·3 = 6.
  • LCM(6, 10, 16): 6=2·3, 10=2·5, 16=2⁴ → LCM = 2⁴·3·5 = 240.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: GCF = common primes with smallest powers; LCM = all primes with biggest powers; and GCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b.

2.2 Rational Numbers

Definition: Any number that can be written as a/b where a, b ∈ ℤ and b ≠ 0. Denoted ℚ.

  • Every integer and natural number is rational (−6 = −6/1, 0 = 0/1).
  • Proper fraction: numerator < denominator. Improper fraction: numerator ≥ denominator. Mixed number: integer + proper fraction.

2.2.1 Decimals

Dividing numerator by denominator gives either:

  • Terminating decimal (division ends, remainder 0). E.g., 3/5 = 0.6.
  • Repeating decimal (remainder never 0, digits repeat). E.g., 5/9 = 0.555… = 0.5̅.

Bar notation marks the repeating block: 1/3 = 0.3̅, 23/99 = 0.2323… = 0.23̅ (both digits under one bar).

Converting terminating decimals to fractions: denominator is a power of 10.

  • 7.3 = 73/10; −0.18 = −18/100 = −9/50.

2.2.2 Converting repeating decimals to fractions

Method: Let d = the decimal. Multiply by a power of 10 so the repeating part aligns, subtract, and solve.

  • 0.5̅: d = 0.5̅ → 10d = 5.5̅ → 10d − d = 5 → 9d = 5 → d = 5/9.
  • 2.12̅ (repeating 12): d = 2.1212… → 100d = 212.12… → 99d = 210 → d = 210/99 = 70/33.
  • 0.12̅ (repeating 2): 100d = 12.2̅, 10d = 1.2̅ → 90d = 11 → d = 11/90.

Representing rational numbers on the number line

Convert fractions to decimals and mark them.

Rational numbers on a number line

Example: Locate −5, 3, 4/3 (=1.3̅), −5/2 (=−2.5). Convert and place each fraction.

2.3 Irrational Numbers

2.3.1 Neither repeating nor terminating

  • Perfect square: a number that is a square of an integer (1, 4, 9, 16, …).
  • A square root of x is a number y such that y² = x. √25 = 5, also −5.
  • √2 ≈ 1.41421356… is neither terminating nor repeating, so it is irrational.

Definition: A decimal that is neither terminating nor repeating is an irrational number. If a is a natural number that is not a perfect square, then √a is irrational.

Examples (rational or irrational?):

  • √25 = 5 → rational.
  • √0.09 = 0.3 → rational.
  • 0.12345… (non-repeating) → irrational.
  • 0.010110111… → irrational.
  • 22/7 → rational (a fraction).
  • π → irrational.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: If a > 0, b > 0 and a < b, then √a < √b. E.g., √5 < √7 since 5 < 7.

Locating √2 on the number line

Use Pythagoras: draw a 1-unit vertical segment at point 1, then the hypotenuse has length √(1²+1²) = √2. With a compass, transfer this length to the number line.

Locating √2 on the number line

2.3.2 Operations on irrational numbers

Rules (a>0, b>0):

  • √a × √b = √(ab)
  • √a ÷ √b = √(a/b)
  • a√b = √(a²b) and √(a²b) = a√b

Examples:

  • √2 × √3 = √6.
  • (2+√2)(1+√5) = 2 + 2√5 + √2 + √10.
  • (√5+√3)² = 5 + 2√15 + 3 = 8 + 2√15.
  • √2/√3 = √(2/3); −√18/√2 = −√9 = −3.
  • √8 + √2 = 2√2 + √2 = 3√2.
  • √18 + √50 = 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2.
  • √72 − √8 = 6√2 − 2√2 = 4√2.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Only like radicals (same index and same radicand) can be combined by addition/subtraction: 2√5 + √5 = 3√5. First simplify so radicals are like.

2.4 Real Numbers

Definition: A number is real if it is rational or irrational. ℝ = ℚ ∪ irrationals.

The real number system
  • Trichotomy: for reals a, b exactly one of a<b, a=b, a>b holds.
  • Transitive: if a<b and b<c then a<c.
  • For non-negative a, b: if a² < b² then a < b.

Examples (compare): −8 < −2; 5/8 = 0.625 < 0.8; √2/3 ≈ 0.471 > 0.34; (√3/6)² = 3/36 < (2/3)² = 16/36, so √3/6 < 2/3.

2.4.1 Intervals

  • Closed [a, b]: a ≤ x ≤ b.
  • Open (a, b): a < x < b.
  • Half-open [a, b) or (a, b]: one endpoint included.
  • Infinity symbols: ∞ (right) and −∞ (left); always written with open parenthesis.
Types of intervals

Examples:

  • Real numbers between 3 and 5 including both → [3, 5].
  • Between −2 and 3/2 including −2, excluding 3/2 → [−2, 3/2).
  • Left of 2 excluding 2 → (−∞, 2).
  • Right of 0 including 0 → [0, ∞).
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Filled/closed dot = included ([ ]); open dot = excluded (( )). ∞ is always open.

2.4.2 Absolute value

|x| = x if x ≥ 0, and |x| = −x if x < 0. It is the distance from 0.

Examples: |4| = 4, |−2| = 2, |1/2| = 1/2, |−0.4| = 0.4, |−√2| = √2, |2 − √8| = √8 − 2 (since √8 > 2).

  • Distance between a and b on the number line = |a − b| = |b − a|.

2.4.3 Exponents and radicals

  • Exponential expression aⁿ: a is the base, n the exponent. 2³ = 8, (−3)⁴ = 81, −2³ = −8.
  • a⁰ = 1 (a≠0); a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
  • Square root / cube root / nth root: if aⁿ = b then a is an nth root of b.
  • Principal nth root √ⁿb: positive nth root if b>0; negative if b<0 and n odd; 0 if b=0.
  • (1/n)th power: b^(1/n) = √ⁿb (for b real and n odd, or b≥0 and n even).
  • a^(m/n) = (a^(1/n))ᵐ.

Laws of exponents (a,b ∈ ℝ, n,m ∈ ℕ):

  • aⁿ × aᵐ = aⁿ⁺ᵐ
  • aⁿ / aᵐ = aⁿ⁻ᵐ (a≠0)
  • (aⁿ)ᵐ = aⁿᵐ
  • (a×b)ⁿ = aⁿ × bⁿ
  • (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ (b≠0)

Examples:

  • 7^(1/2) × 7^(3/2) = 7² = 49.
  • (25×9)^(1/2) = 5×3 = 15.
  • (8/27)^(1/3) = 2/3.
  • √50 = 5√2.

Addition/subtraction of like radicals: √3 + √12 = √3 + 2√3 = 3√3; 2√18 − √2 + √8 = 6√2 − √2 + 2√2 = 7√2.

Operations on real numbers:

  • Sum/difference/product/quotient of two rationals → rational (rationals are closed under +, −, ×, ÷).
  • Sum of rational and irrational → irrational.
  • Product of non-zero rational and irrational → irrational.

Properties of ℝ: closure, commutative, associative, identity (0 and 1), inverse (additive −a, multiplicative 1/a), distributive a(b+c) = ab+ac.

Examples of inverses: additive inverse of √2 is −√2, multiplicative inverse is 1/√2; additive inverse of 3/4 is −3/4, multiplicative is 4/3; additive inverse of 0.5 is −0.5, multiplicative is 2.

2.4.4 Limit of accuracy

  • Rounding: if the next digit is 0–4, keep; if 5–9, round up.
  • 38,721 to nearest 100 → 38,700; to nearest 1000 → 39,000; to nearest 10,000 → 40,000.
  • Decimal places (d.p.): 10.673 to 1 d.p. → 10.7; 3.173 to 2 d.p. → 3.17.
  • Significant figures (s.f.): 2.364 to 2 s.f. → 2.4; 0.0062 to 1 s.f. → 0.006; 0.3041 to 2 s.f. → 0.30.
  • Lower/upper bound: bound = value ± (place value ÷ 2).
  • 872 kg to nearest kg: lower 871.5, upper 872.5; as inequality 871.5 ≤ wt < 872.5.
  • 10.7 to 1 d.p.: lower 10.65, upper 10.75.
  • Effect of operations: for sums/products, lower bound = sum/product of lower bounds; upper = sum/product of upper bounds.
  • Field 12 m × 6 m: 11.5 ≤ l < 12.5, 5.5 ≤ w < 6.5; sum between 17 and 19; area between 63.25 and 81.25.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Lower/upper bound = value ± ½×(place value). For + and ×, min uses the lower bounds and max uses the upper bounds.

2.4.5 Standard (scientific) notation

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10 and n an integer.

  • 1,856,700,000 = 1.8567 × 10⁹.
  • 0.000000314 = 3.14 × 10⁻⁷.
  • 5.37 × 10⁶ = 5,370,000; 1.7 × 10⁻⁷ = 0.00000017.

2.4.6 Rationalization

Change an irrational denominator into a rational one by multiplying by the rationalizing factor (= 1).

  • 2/√3 × √3/√3 = 2√3/3.
  • √2/√5 × √5/√5 = √10/5.
  • 1/√2³ × √2²/√2² = √2²/2 = √4/2.

For sums with radicals use the conjugate:

  • 1/(√2+1) × (√2−1)/(√2−1) = √2 − 1.
  • 3/(√5−√3) × (√5+√3)/(√5+√3) = 3(√5+√3)/2.
  • Useful: (√a−√b)(√a+√b) = a−b; (a+√b)(a−√b) = a²−b.

2.5 Applications

Example 1: 530 flower pots in rows of 21 → 530 = 21×25 + 5 → 25 rows, 5 pots left over.

Example 2: Cover a 50 cm × 20 cm board with largest square tiles → GCF(50,20) = 10 cm tiles (50 = 2·5², 20 = 2²·5, GCF = 2·5 = 10).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Word problems with "largest equal pieces / rooms / teams" use GCF; problems with "when will they meet again / smallest common" use LCM.

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 2)

  • Euclid: a = bq + r, 0 ≤ r < b.
  • Prime (2 factors) vs composite (>2); 1 is neither; 2 is the only even prime.
  • Divisibility rules for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10.
  • Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: unique prime factorization.
  • GCF (least powers) and LCM (greatest powers); GCF × LCM = a×b.
  • Rational ℚ = a/b; terminating or repeating decimals.
  • Irrational = non-terminating, non-repeating; √a irrational if a not a perfect square.
  • ℝ = rational ∪ irrational.
  • Radicals: √a·√b=√ab, √a/√b=√(a/b), a√b=√(a²b).
  • Exponents laws; a⁰=1; a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ.
  • Absolute value |x|; distance = |a−b|.
  • Scientific notation a×10ⁿ, 1≤a<10.
  • Bounds = value ± ½(place value).
  • Rationalize denominators using conjugate.

UNIT 3: SOLVING EQUATIONS

Note: Based on the official FDRE MoE Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook (New Curriculum, 2023), Unit 3.

3.1 Revision on Linear Equation in One Variable

Definition: An equation in one variable with exponent 1 is linear, of the form ax + b = 0 (a, b real, a≠0). It has exactly one solution.

Steps to solve:

  1. Clear fractions using the LCM.
  2. Simplify both sides.
  3. Isolate the variable.
  4. Verify the answer.

Examples:

  • x + 2 = 0 → x = −2.
  • 3x + 4 = 10 → 3x = 6 → x = 2.
  • (5/4)x + 1/2 = 2x − 1/2 → multiply by 4 → 5x + 2 = 8x − 2 → x = 4/3.

Worked problem: An isosceles triangle has each leg 6 cm more than the base; perimeter = 54 cm. Let base = a, each leg = a+6. Then a + 2(a+6) = 54 → 3a + 12 = 54 → a = 14. So base = 14 cm, legs = 20 cm each.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: A linear equation in one variable, ax + b = 0 (a≠0), has exactly one solution.

3.2 Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables

Definition: A linear equation in two variables: ax + by = c (a≠0, b≠0). Its graph is a straight line; it has infinitely many solutions (all points on the line).

A system of two linear equations in two variables can have:

  • One solution (lines intersect) — independent system, a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂.
  • No solution (lines parallel) — inconsistent, a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂.
  • Infinitely many (lines coincide) — dependent, a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂.

3.2.1 Solving using tables

Solve each equation for y, make a table of x and y, find the pair satisfying both.

Example: {2x + y = 15; 3x − y = 5} → y = −2x + 15 and y = 3x − 5. The ordered pair (4, 7) satisfies both.

3.2.2 Substitution method

  1. Solve one equation for one variable.
  2. Substitute into the other equation.
  3. Solve for the second variable.
  4. Substitute back for the first.
  5. Check.

Example: {−x + y = −5; 2x − 5y = 1}. From first, y = x − 5. Substitute: 2x − 5(x−5) = 1 → −3x + 25 = 1 → x = 8. Then y = 3. Solution: (8, 3).

3.2.3 Elimination (addition) method

Eliminate one variable by adding equations whose coefficients are opposites; multiply by a constant first if needed.

Example 1: {x + 2y = 1; −x + y = 5}. Adding: 3y = 6 → y = 2. Then x = −3. Solution: (−3, 2).

Example 2: {4x + 2y = 28; x + 2y = 13}. Subtract (or add after multiplying second by −1): 3x = 15 → x = 5, then y = 4. Solution: (5, 4).

Example 3: {3x + 4y = 2; x − 2y = 4}. Multiply second by −3: {3x+4y=2; −3x+6y=−12}. Add: 10y = −10 → y = −1, then x = 2. Solution: (2, −1).

Word problem: Three pens + two books = Birr 118; one pen + two books = Birr 106. Let p = pen, b = book. {3p+2b=118; p+2b=106}. From second p = 106 − 2b. Substitute: 3(106−2b)+2b=118 → 318−6b+2b=118 → −4b=−200 → b=50, p=6. So a pen is Birr 6, a book Birr 50.

3.2.4 Graphical method

  1. Graph the first equation.
  2. Graph the second on the same axes.
  3. Determine whether lines intersect, are parallel, or coincide.
  4. The intersection point is the solution.
Intersecting lines — one solution
Parallel lines — no solution
Coincident lines — infinite solutions

Example 1: {2x + y = −8; x − y = −1} → y = −2x−8 and y = x+1. Lines intersect at (−3, −2).

Example 2: {2x − y = −1; 4x − 2y = −8} → y = 2x+1 and y = 2x+4. Parallel → no solution.

Example 3: {3x + y = 6; 6x + 2y = 12} → both give y = −3x+6 → coincident → infinite solutions.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know — classify systems by ratios:
Note: - a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ → infinite solutions (dependent/coincident).
Note: - a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ → no solution (inconsistent/parallel).
Note: - a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ → one solution (independent/intersect).

3.3 Solving Nonlinear Equations

3.3.1 Equations involving absolute value

  • |p| = |−p|; |p| ≥ 0.
  • For p ≥ 0: |x| = p means x = p or x = −p.
  • An absolute value equation has no solution if the absolute value equals a negative number (|x| = −1 has none).

Examples:

  • |x| = 4 → x = 4 or x = −4.
  • |x + 7| = 14 → x + 7 = 14 or x + 7 = −14 → x = 7 or x = −21.
  • 2|2x−1| − 1 = 5 → |2x−1| = 3 → 2x−1 = 3 or 2x−1 = −3 → x = 2 or x = −1.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: |x| = p (p ≥ 0) → x = p or x = −p. If |expression| = negative, there is NO solution.

3.3.2 Quadratic equations

Definition: ax² + bx + c = 0 with a, b, c ∈ ℝ and a ≠ 0. a = leading coefficient, b = middle-term coefficient, c = constant.

Methods:

  1. Factorization (set each factor to zero, use ab = 0 ⟺ a = 0 or b = 0).
  • x² − 6x − 16 = 0 → (x − 8)(x + 2) = 0 → x = 8 or x = −2.
  • x² + 6x + 9 = 0 → (x+3)² = 0 → x = −3 (one solution).
  • x² − 9 = 0 → (x−3)(x+3) = 0 → x = ±3.
  • 4x² + 4x + 1 = 0 → (2x+1)² = 0 → x = −1/2.
  1. Completing the square — add and subtract (b/2a)².
  • x² + 6x + 4 = 0 → (x+3)² − 5 = 0 → x = −3 ± √5.
  • x² + 6x + 7 = 0 → (x+3)² − 2 = 0 → x = −3 ± √2.
  1. Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / (2a).
  • x² − 6x + 3 = 0 → x = [6 ± √(36−12)]/2 = 3 ± √6.

Discriminant D = b² − 4ac:

  • D > 0 → two distinct real roots.
  • D = 0 → exactly one real root (equal roots).
  • D < 0 → no real roots.

Examples:

  • x² + 2x + 2 = 0: D = 4 − 8 = −4 < 0 → no real roots.
  • x² + 18x + 81 = 0: D = 0 → one root, x = −9.
  • x² + 4x + 3 = 0: D = 4 > 0 → two roots, x = −1, −3.

Relations between roots and coefficients: for roots r₁, r₂:

  • r₁ + r₂ = −b/a
  • r₁ · r₂ = c/a

Example: For ax² + 6x + c = 0, if sum = −6/5 and product = 1/5: −6/a = −6/5 → a = 5; c/5 = 1/5 → c = 1. Equation: 5x² + 6x + 1 = 0.

3.3.3 Equations involving exponents and radicals

Exponent equations: for a > 0, aˣ = aʸ ⟺ x = y (make bases equal).

Examples:

  • 2ˣ = 8 = 2³ → x = 3.
  • 3ˣ = 1/27 = 3⁻³ → x = −3.
  • 8ˣ = 16 → 2³ˣ = 2⁴ → 3x = 4 → x = 4/3.
  • 2ˣ⁺⁴ = 32 = 2⁵ → x + 4 = 5 → x = 1.
  • 9ˣ⁺⁴ = 27 → 3²⁽ˣ⁺⁴⁾ = 3³ → 2x + 8 = 3 → x = −5/2.
  • (x² + 6x)^(1/4) = 2 → raise to 4th power → x² + 6x = 16 → x² + 6x − 16 = 0 → x = −8, 2.

Radical equations: contain variables in the radicand.

Steps: specify domain (radicand ≥ 0), isolate the radical, square/raise both sides, solve, verify.

Examples:

  • √(15−2x) = x: domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 15/2. Square: 15 − 2x = x² → x² + 2x − 15 = 0 → x = 3 or x = −5. Only x = 3 valid.
  • √(x+3) = 3x − 1: domain x ≥ 1/3. Square: x+3 = 9x²−6x+1 → 9x²−7x−2=0 → x=1 or x=−2/9. Only x = 1 valid.
  • √(2x+3) + √(x−2) = 4: domain x ≥ 2. Solve → x = 3 (x = 83 rejected).
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Always check solutions to radical/exponent equations against the domain. A "solution" that makes a radicand negative is rejected.

3.4 Applications of Solving Equations

System application: Circus tickets Birr 25 (children) / Birr 50 (adults); 2,000 attendees, revenue Birr 70,000.

  • c + a = 2000; 25c + 50a = 70000.
  • a = 2000 − c → 25c + 50(2000−c) = 70000 → −25c = −30000 → c = 1200, a = 800.
  • Answer: 1,200 children and 800 adults.

Quadratic application: Object dropped from 600 m, h = 600 − 16t². Time to reach 200 m:

  • t = √((600−h)/4)... t² = (600−200)/16 = 25 → t = 5 seconds.

Projectile: h = −16t² + 48t + 64. Hits ground when h = 0: 0 = −16(t² − 3t − 4) = −16(t+1)(t−4) → t = 4 seconds (t = −1 rejected).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: In word problems, define variables, build the equation(s), solve, and reject impossible answers (negative time, etc.).

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 3)

  • Linear (1 var) ax + b = 0 → one solution.
  • Linear (2 vars) ax + by = c → line, infinite solutions.
  • System methods: table, substitution, elimination, graphical.
  • System classification by coefficient ratios (dependent/inconsistent/independent).
  • |x| = p → x = ±p; |x| = negative → no solution.
  • Quadratic ax²+bx+c=0; solve by factorization, completing square, or formula x=(−b±√D)/2a.
  • Discriminant D = b²−4ac (2 / 1 / 0 real roots).
  • Sum of roots = −b/a, product = c/a.
  • aˣ = aʸ ⟺ x = y.
  • Radical equations: isolate, raise power, check domain & verify.

UNIT 4: SOLVING INEQUALITIES

Note: Based on the official FDRE MoE Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook (New Curriculum, 2023), Unit 4.

4.1 Revision on Linear Inequalities in One Variable

An algebraic inequality connects an expression to another with <, ≤, >, or ≥.

Properties:

  • If a > b then a + c > b + c and a − c > b − c.
  • If a > b and m > 0 then ma > mb and a/m > b/m (positive: sign unchanged).
  • If a > b and m < 0 then ma < mb and a/m < b/m (negative: REVERSE the sign).

Examples:

  • x − 5 > 2 → x > 7.
  • 2x > 4 → x > 2.
  • (1/3)x < 1 → x < 3.
  • −3x > 6 → x < −2 (divided by negative, reversed).
  • 2x − 3 ≥ 1 → x ≥ 2.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. This is the most common error in this unit.

Intervals on the number line

  • Closed [a, b]: a ≤ x ≤ b (filled dots).
  • Open (a, b): a < x < b (open dots).
  • Half-open [a, b) or (a, b].

Examples:

  • x + 1 > −2 → x > −3 → interval (−3, ∞). Open dot at −3.
  • 3x − (x+2) ≥ 0 → 2x ≥ 2 → x ≥ 1 → interval [1, ∞). Closed dot at 1.
Number lines for linear inequalities

Examples with intervals:

  • x + 2 < −x + 6 → 2x < 4 → x < 2 → (−∞, 2).
  • −(2/3)x + 1/2 ≤ 5/6 → multiply by 6: −4x + 3 ≤ 5 → −4x ≤ 2 → x ≥ −1/2 (reversed). Interval [−1/2, ∞).
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Open dot (excluded) vs closed dot (included). ∞ is always written with an open parenthesis.

4.2 Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables

Linear inequalities in two variables represent the unequal relation between two expressions in two variables.

Graphing procedure:

  1. Sketch the corresponding boundary line (equation).
  2. Use a solid line if ≤ or ≥ (points on line are solutions); dashed if < or >.
  3. Choose a test point not on the line (usually (0,0) unless on the line); if it satisfies the inequality, shade that side; otherwise shade the other side.
  4. For a system, the solution is the overlap (intersection) of the shaded regions.

Example 1: y > −x — dashed line y = −x, shade above.

Example 2: {y < 2x + 5; y > −x} — dashed lines, solution is the overlapping (dark) region.

System of linear inequalities

Example 3: {y ≤ x − 2; y > −3x + 5} — solid y = x−2 (shade below, since (0,0) fails), dashed y = −3x+5 (shade the side not containing (0,0)). Solution is the intersection.

Example 4: {2x + 3y ≥ 12; x − 4y > 1; x < 4} — rewrite as y ≥ −(2/3)x + 4 (solid, upper), y < (1/2)x − 1/4 (dashed, lower), x < 4 (dashed vertical, left). Solution is the triple overlap.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: solid ≤/≥, dashed </>. Test a point (e.g., (0,0)) to decide which side to shade. System solution = overlap of shadings.

4.3 Inequalities Involving Absolute Value

Rules (c > 0):

  • |k| < c → −c < k < c.
  • |k| ≤ c → −c ≤ k ≤ c.
  • |k| > c → k > c or k < −c.
  • |k| ≥ c → k ≥ c or k ≤ −c.
Absolute value inequalities

Examples:

  • |x| ≤ 1 → −1 ≤ x ≤ 1.
  • |x| > 1 → x < −1 or x > 1.
  • |x + 2| < 4 → −4 < x + 2 < 4 → −6 < x < 2 → interval (−6, 2).
  • |x + 2| ≥ 4 → x ≤ −6 or x ≥ 2 → (−∞, −6] ∪ [2, ∞).
  • |3x − 2| ≥ 7 → 3x − 2 ≥ 7 or 3x − 2 ≤ −7 → x ≥ 3 or x ≤ −5/3.
  • |−x + 4| < 0 → no solution (absolute value can't be negative).
  • |−5x − 7| ≤ 0 → equals zero: −5x − 7 = 0 → x = −7/5 (one solution).
  • |6x + | > −2 → all real numbers (absolute value always > a negative).
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: |k| < c gives a "between" (compound) answer; |k| > c gives a "split" (union) answer. Watch ≤/≥ for closed intervals and open dots.

4.4 Quadratic Inequalities

Definition: General forms ax² + bx + c < 0, ≤ 0, > 0, ≥ 0 (a ≠ 0).

4.4.1 Product properties

  • m·n > 0 iff (m > 0 and n > 0) or (m < 0 and n < 0).
  • m·n < 0 iff (m > 0 and n < 0) or (m < 0 and n > 0).

Examples:

  • (x−3)(x−1) < 0 → case 2: x−3<0 and x−1>0 → x<3 and x>1 → 1 < x < 3 → (1, 3).
  • (x−4)(x−2) > 0 → x>4 or x<2 → (−∞, 2) ∪ (4, ∞).
  • x² − x ≥ 12 → x² − x − 12 ≥ 0 → (x−4)(x+3) ≥ 0 → x ≥ 4 or x ≤ −3 → (−∞, −3] ∪ [4, ∞).
  • −x² + x + 12 ≤ 0 → x² − x − 12 ≥ 0 → same: x ≤ −3 or x ≥ 4.

4.4.2 Sign chart method

Factorize, find key points (roots), and test the sign of each factor in each interval.

Example: (x−4)(x+3) < 0

  • Roots: x = −3, x = 4.
  • Intervals: x<−3, −3<x<4, x>4.
Factorx<−3−3<x<4x>4
x−4−−+
x+3−++
(x−4)(x+3)+−+
  • Product < 0 on −3 < x < 4 → solution (−3, 4).

Example: (x+3)(x+2) ≥ 0 → product ≥ 0 on x ≤ −3 or x ≥ −2 → (−∞, −3] ∪ [−2, ∞).

Quadratic inequality parabola

(Graphically, x²−x−12 ≥ 0 where the parabola is on/above the x-axis, i.e., x ≤ −3 or x ≥ 4.)

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: A quadratic inequality can be solved by product property, sign chart, or graph. For ">0" the answer is two outside intervals; for "<0" the answer is the between interval.

4.5 Applications of Inequalities

Example 1: Kebede has Birr 6,000, saves Birr 1,000/month until > 80,000. 6000 + 1000m > 80000 → 1000m > 74000 → m > 74. So more than 74 months (6 years 2 months).

Example 2: Chaltu charged Birr 0.20/message, has Birr 50, bill ≤ Birr 80. 0.2m + 50 ≤ 80 → 0.2m ≤ 30 → m ≤ 150. Max 150 messages.

Example 3: Normal pregnancy 37 to 41 weeks inclusive: 37 ≤ w ≤ 41. Abnormal: w < 37 or w > 41.

Example 4: Dendir: food service Birr 10/hr + tutoring Birr 15/hr, needs ≥ Birr 240. 10x + 15y ≥ 240 → y ≥ −(2/3)x + 16. Shade the upper region; e.g., (15,10), (0,16), (24,0) are solutions.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: "at most" → ≤; "at least / more than" → ≥ or >; "between, inclusive" → compound a ≤ x ≤ b.

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 4)

  • Negative multiplier reverses the inequality sign.
  • Solid ≤/≥, dashed </>; shade the correct side using a test point.
  • |k| < c → −c < k < c (between). |k| > c → k > c or k < −c (split).
  • Quadratic inequality methods: product property, sign chart, graph.
  • Product: m·n>0 if same signs; m·n<0 if opposite signs.
  • Applications: "at least" ≥, "at most" ≤.

UNIT 5: INTRODUCTION TO TRIGONOMETRY

Note: Based on the official FDRE MoE Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook (New Curriculum, 2023), Unit 5.

5.1 Revision on Right-Angled Triangles

Definition: A right-angled triangle has one angle equal to 90°.

Properties:

  • The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse (always the longest side).
  • The other two sides adjacent to the right angle are the base and the perpendicular side.
  • The sum of the other two interior angles is 90° (each acute).
  • Pythagoras theorem: b² + p² = h² (b = base, p = perpendicular, h = hypotenuse).
Right-angled triangle

Examples:

  • Missing side: x² + 4² = 6² → x² = 20 → x = 2√5.
  • Height of an equilateral triangle of side 6: draw altitude → right triangle with hypotenuse 6 and base 3 → 3² + x² = 6² → x² = 27 → x = 3√3.

Conversion of Pythagoras: if b² + p² = h², then the angle between b and p is 90°.

Check which are right-angled:

  • 5, 6, 2: 5² + 2² = 29 ≠ 6² = 36 → NOT right-angled.
  • 3, 4, 5: 3² + 4² = 25 = 5² → right-angled.
  • √5, 2, 3: (√5)² + 2² = 9 = 3² → right-angled.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Pythagoras: b² + p² = h². The hypotenuse is always the longest side, opposite the 90° angle.

5.2 Trigonometric Ratios

Definition: The trigonometric ratios of an acute angle are ratios of two sides of a right-angled triangle. They depend only on the angle, not the size of the triangle.

For angle A in the right triangle (hypotenuse AC, opposite BC, adjacent AB):

  • sin A = opposite / hypotenuse = BC/AC
  • cos A = adjacent / hypotenuse = AB/AC
  • tan A = opposite / adjacent = BC/AB
  • tan A = sin A / cos A

Example: If sin A = 3/5, draw the triangle (BC = 3, AC = 5), then AB = √(25−9) = 4. So cos A = 4/5, tan A = 3/4.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: SOH-CAH-TOA:
Note: - sin = Opposite/Hypotenuse
Note: - cos = Adjacent/Hypotenuse
Note: - tan = Opposite/Adjacent

Trigonometric values of basic angles

45° (isosceles right triangle, legs = a, hyp = a√2):

  • sin 45° = 1/√2, cos 45° = 1/√2, tan 45° = 1.
45-45-90 triangle

30° and 60° (half of an equilateral triangle, e.g., sides 1, √3, 2):

  • sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3.
  • sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3.
30-60-90 triangle

Complete table of basic values:

Anglesincostan
0°010
30°1/2√3/21/√3
45°1/√21/√21
60°√3/21/2√3

Remark: As the angle goes from 0° to 90°, sin increases 0→1, cos decreases 1→0, tan increases 0→∞ (1 at 45°).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Memorize the table! Pattern for sin row: 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1 (i.e., √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2). Cos row is sin reversed.

Using the trigonometric table

  • For angles 0°–45° read from the top row; for 45°–90° read from the bottom row.
  • sin 18° ≈ 0.309017; cos 37° ≈ 0.798636; tan 70° ≈ 2.747480.
  • Given cos A = 0.819152 → A = 35°.
  • Given sin A = 0.7565 → nearest degree is 49° (0.75471).

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 5)

  • Right triangle: b² + p² = h²; hypotenuse longest, opposite 90°.
  • sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj.
  • Basic angles table (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°).
  • sin A = cos(90°−A); cos A = sin(90°−A).
  • tan 90° is undefined.
  • Read trig values from the table for any acute angle.

UNIT 6: REGULAR POLYGONS

Note: Based on the official FDRE MoE Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook (New Curriculum, 2023), Unit 6.

6.1 Sum of Interior Angles of a Convex Polygon

Definition: A polygon is a simple closed plane figure formed by three or more line segments joined end to end, no two in succession collinear. The line segments are sides, their common endpoints are vertices, and the angles inside are interior angles.

Polygon names: Triangle (3), Quadrilateral (4), Pentagon (5), Hexagon (6), Heptagon (7), Octagon (8), Nonagon (9), Decagon (10). A polygon with n sides is an "n-gon."

Convex vs concave:

  • Convex: every interior angle < 180° (vertices point outwards).
  • Concave: at least one interior angle > 180° (a vertex points inwards).

Sum of interior angles of an n-sided polygon = (n − 2) × 180°.

Reasoning: Drawing all diagonals from one vertex divides the polygon into (n − 2) triangles, each with 180°.

Examples:

  • Quadrilateral: (4−2)×180° = 360° (2 triangles).
  • Pentagon: (5−2)×180° = 540° (3 triangles).
  • Hexagon: (6−2)×180° = 720°.
  • If sum = 1,080°, then (n−2)×180 = 1080 → n−2 = 6 → n = 8 (octagon).
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Sum of interior angles of n-gon = (n−2)×180°.

6.2 Sum of Exterior Angles of a Convex Polygon

Definition: An exterior angle is the angle outside the polygon formed by one side and the extension of an adjacent side.

Sum of the exterior angles of any polygon = 360°.

Reasoning: interior + exterior at each vertex = 180° (a straight line), so (sum of interior) + (sum of exterior) = n×180°. Since sum of interior = (n−2)×180°, the exterior sum = n×180° − (n−2)×180° = 360°.

Example: A triangle with interior angles 60°, 40°, and 80° has exterior angles 120°, 140°, 100°; their sum is 360°.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: The sum of exterior angles is always 360° regardless of the number of sides.

6.3 Measures of Each Interior and Exterior Angle of a Regular Polygon

Definition: A polygon is regular if it is equiangular (equal angles) and equilateral (equal sides). E.g., equilateral triangles, squares, regular hexagons (honeycomb).

For a regular n-gon:

  • Each interior angle = (n−2)×180° / n.
  • Each exterior angle = 360° / n.
  • Interior + exterior at each vertex = 180°.

Example — regular pentagon (n = 5):

  • Each interior angle = 3×180°/5 = 108°.
  • Each exterior angle = 360°/5 = 72°.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Interior = (n−2)×180°/n; exterior = 360°/n. They sum to 180°.

6.4 Properties of Regular Polygons: Pentagon, Hexagon, Octagon, Decagon

Lines of symmetry

  • A line of symmetry is a line through which the two halves of a figure match exactly (mirror line).
  • An n-sided regular polygon has n lines of symmetry.
  • The lines of symmetry meet at the center of the polygon.
  • If n is odd, lines connect vertex to side; if n is even, lines connect vertex to vertex and side to side.
Regular polygons
Regular hexagon with lines of symmetry

Example: A regular heptagon (7 sides) has 7 lines of symmetry.

Inscribed and circumscribed polygons

  • Circumcircle: the circle passing through all vertices (polygon is inscribed in it).
  • Incircle: the circle inside the polygon touching each side at its midpoint.
  • Apothem (a): the perpendicular segment from the center to the midpoint of a side.
  • A circle can always be inscribed in / circumscribed about any regular polygon.
Inscribed regular hexagon with apothem

Central angle

  • The central angle is the angle at the center formed by two radii to adjacent vertices.
  • Each central angle = 360° / n.
  • The central angles divide the polygon into n congruent isosceles triangles.

Examples: n = 5 → 72°; n = 8 → 45°; if central angle = 12°, then n = 360/12 = 30 sides.

Perimeter, area, and apothem of a regular polygon inscribed in a circle of radius r

Theorem 6.1: For an n-sided regular polygon inscribed in a circle of radius r:

  • s = 2r sin(180°/n) (side length)
  • a = r cos(180°/n) (apothem)
  • P = 2nr sin(180°/n) (perimeter)
  • A = ½ aP (area)

Example — regular hexagon (n=6): central angle = 60°, so triangle AOB is equilateral: s = r, P = 6r. Apothem a = r cos 30° = (√3/2)r. Area = 6 × (√3/4)r² = (3√3/2)r².

Example 2: Square inscribed in radius 5 cm: s = 2(5) sin 45° = 5√2 cm.

Example 2b: Apothem of regular pentagon, radius 6 cm: a = 6 cos 36° ≈ 6×0.809 = 4.854 cm.

Example 2c: Area of regular nonagon, radius 10 cm: A = 9(100) cos 20° sin 20° ≈ 289.24 cm².

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: s = 2r sin(180°/n), a = r cos(180°/n), P = 2nr sin(180°/n), A = ½ aP. The central angle = 360°/n.

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 6)

  • Sum of interior angles = (n−2)×180°.
  • Sum of exterior angles = 360° (always).
  • Regular n-gon: interior = (n−2)×180°/n, exterior = 360°/n, central = 360°/n.
  • Interior + exterior = 180° at each vertex.
  • n lines of symmetry for a regular n-gon.
  • Inscribed polygon formulas: s = 2r sin(180°/n), a = r cos(180°/n), P = 2nr sin(180°/n), A = ½ aP.
  • Apothem = perpendicular from center to side midpoint.

UNIT 7: CONGRUENCY AND SIMILARITY

Note: Based on the official FDRE MoE Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook (New Curriculum, 2023), Unit 7.

7.1 Revision on Congruency of Triangles

Definition: Two triangles are congruent if they have exactly the same three sides and the same three angles — identical in size and shape.

Notation: △ABC ≡ △DEF means AB ≡ DE, BC ≡ EF, AC ≡ DF and ∠A≡∠D, ∠B≡∠E, ∠C≡∠F.

Congruent triangles

Congruence postulates/criteria:

  1. SSS — three pairs of equal sides.
  2. SAS — two pairs of sides equal and the included angle equal.
  3. ASA — two angles and the included side equal.
  4. RHS — for right triangles: equal hypotenuse and one leg.

Example: If △ABC ≡ △DEF, ∠A = 45°, ∠C = 85°, then ∠B = 50°; so ∠D = 45°, ∠E = 50°, ∠F = 85°.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Congruent = same size and shape. Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS. "Included" means between the two sides/angles.

7.2 Definition of Similar Figures

Definition: Two plane figures are similar if their corresponding angles are congruent and the ratios of their corresponding sides are proportional. This common ratio is called the scale factor.

Notation: △ABC ~ △DEF.

  • Any two circles are similar. Any two squares are similar. Any two regular polygons (with the same number of sides) are similar.
  • All equilateral triangles are similar; all squares are similar.
  • All isosceles triangles are NOT necessarily similar; all rectangles are NOT necessarily similar.

Example: If △ABC ~ △DEF with sides 4, 5, 2 and 8, 10, 4, the common ratio (scale factor) = 2 (8/4 = 10/5 = 4/2 = 2).

Similar triangles
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Similar = same shape, proportional sides, equal angles. Scale factor = ratio of corresponding sides.

7.3 Theorems on Similar Plane Figures

Similarity theorems (for triangles):

  1. AA (Angle-Angle): if two angles of one triangle are equal to two angles of another, the triangles are similar (the third angle is automatic). (Equiangular triangles are similar.)
  2. SSS: if the three corresponding sides are proportional, the triangles are similar.
  3. SAS: if two corresponding sides are proportional and the included angle is equal, the triangles are similar.

AA example: If m∠G = 48° and m∠M = 30° matching two angles, then △EFG ~ △LMN by AA.

SSS example: AB/DE = BC/EF = AC/DF = 2 → △ABC ~ △DEF.

SAS example: AB/DE = 12/6 = 2, AC/DF = 14/7 = 2, and ∠A = ∠D → △ABC ~ △DEF.

Using similarity to find missing sides: Since △ABC ~ △DEF, set up ratios. E.g., if AB/DE = BC/EF = AC/DF, use known values to solve for unknowns.

Find an angle: If △ABC ~ △DEF, corresponding angles are equal. Match longest with longest, shortest with shortest.

Pythagoras via similarity: In a right triangle ABC, drawing BD perpendicular to AC creates three similar right triangles (△ABC ~ △ADB ~ △BDC), which can prove b² + p² = h².

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: AA, SSS, and SAS similarity. "Included" angle in SAS is between the two proportional sides.

7.4 Ratio of Perimeters of Similar Plane Figures

Definition: If two figures are similar, the ratio of their perimeters equals the ratio of their corresponding side lengths (the scale factor).

Example: △ABC has sides 6, 8, 10 (P = 24); △DEF has sides 3, 4, 5 (P = 12). Ratio of perimeters = 24/12 = 2 = scale factor.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: P₁/P₂ = s₁/s₂ (perimeters scale by the scale factor).

7.5 Ratio of Areas of Similar Plane Figures

Definition: If two figures are similar, the ratio of their areas equals the square of the ratio of their corresponding side lengths (scale factor²).

Example: Similar rectangles 1×2 and 3×6: side ratio 3, area ratio = 3² = 9. Indeed areas 2 and 18 → ratio 9.

Example: If triangles are similar with corresponding sides 6 and 10, area ratio = (10/6)² = 25/9.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Perimeter ratio = k; Area ratio = k².

7.6 Construction of Similar Figures

To construct a triangle similar to a given △ABC with scale factor 5/3:

  1. Draw a ray BX making an acute angle with BC; mark 5 equal segments B₁…B₅.
  2. Join B₃C; draw B₅C′ parallel to B₃C.
  3. Draw a line through C′ parallel to AC to meet BA produced at A′.
  4. △A′B′C′ is similar to △ABC with scale factor 5/3.
  • Scale factor > 1 → larger figure; < 1 → smaller; = 1 → congruent.

7.7 Applications of Similarity

Similar triangles measure heights and distances of tall objects without climbing.

Example 1: Almaz is 1.6 m tall, shadow 2 m; brother's shadow 1.5 m. By proportionality: x/1.6 = 1.5/2 → x = 1.2 m.

Example 2: Building 35 m above water; observer 10 m from edge, eye level 1.8 m above top; align with boat. 35/1.8 = x/10 → x ≈ 194.4 m.

Example 3 (buildings): Given DC = 1, BC = 3, CF = 4, AB = 2; extend FA and CB to meet at G; use △DGE ~ △CGF and △AGB ~ △FGC → find the height x = 14/3.

Example 4 (river width): Person A moves 15 m, B moves 60 m; A moves 5 m from river. Using similar triangles: 15/60 = 5/FC → FC = 20 m (river width).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: For shadow/height problems, set up ratios of corresponding sides of similar triangles.

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 7)

  • Congruent: same size & shape (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS).
  • Similar: same shape, proportional sides, equal angles (AA, SSS, SAS).
  • Perimeter ratio = scale factor k.
  • Area ratio = k².
  • Applications: shadows, building heights, river widths use similar-triangle proportions.

UNIT 8: VECTORS IN TWO DIMENSIONS

Note: Based on the official FDRE MoE Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook (New Curriculum, 2023), Unit 8.

8.1 Vector and Scalar Quantities

Definition: Scalars are quantities fully described by a magnitude (numerical value) alone. E.g., mass (10 kg), density (1 g/cm³), temperature (27 °C), distance, speed, area.

Definition: Vectors are quantities fully described by both a magnitude and a direction. E.g., force, velocity, acceleration, displacement, weight.

Examples:

  • Distance (scalar) vs displacement (vector — distance with direction).
  • Force of 10 N applied upward vs horizontally produce different effects → force is a vector.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Scalars: magnitude only. Vectors: magnitude + direction. Displacement is a "directed distance."

8.2 Representation of a Vector

  • A vector is represented geometrically by a directed line segment with an arrow, e.g., AB→ (A = initial point, B = terminal point).
  • Represented algebraically by letters with arrows (ū, v̄) or bold letters (a, u), or as a column vector.
Column vector

Column vector: any vector ā can be written as ā = (x, y), where x = horizontal component, y = vertical component. E.g., ā = (2, 3).

Equality of vectors

Two vectors are equal if and only if they have the same magnitude and direction. AB→ = CD→ if they are equal.

Opposite of a vector

The vector with the same magnitude but opposite direction is the negative of the vector, −ā. So a = −(−a); AB→ = −CD→ if opposite.

Parallel vectors

Vectors with the same or opposite direction are parallel.

Magnitude of a vector

  • If ā = (x, y), then |ā| = √(x² + y²).
  • For AB→ with A=(x₁,y₁), B=(x₂,y₂): |AB→| = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²) (distance formula).

Example: |ū| for ū = (4,3) → |ū| = √(16+9) = √25 = 5 units.

Example (coordinates): |AB→| with A=(2,2), B=(3,7) → √((3−2)²+(7−2)²) = √26.

Direction of a vector

The direction is the angle the vector makes with a reference direction (horizontal or vertical). Express as North/South, angle, East/West.

Example: A vector at 37° to the horizontal, with y-axis = North and x-axis = East, has complement 53°, so its direction is N 53° E.

8.3 Vector Operations

8.3.1 Addition of vectors

Triangle law: AB→ + BC→ = AC→. The sum (resultant) is the third side of the triangle formed by placing the initial of the second at the terminal of the first.

Triangle law of vector addition

Parallelogram law: For two co-initial vectors, construct a parallelogram; the diagonal from the common initial point is the sum.

Parallelogram law

Example: FH→ + HG→ = FG→. EF→ + FG→ = EG→ and GH→ + HE→ = GE→ (parallel and opposite).

Subtraction of vectors: a − b = a + (−b). Draw the first vector, then from its terminal draw the opposite of the second; the resultant joins initial of first to terminal of the second.

Addition/subtraction of column vectors:

  • (p, q) + (r, s) = (p+r, q+s).
  • (p, q) − (r, s) = (p−r, q−s).

Example: ā = (−4, −3), b̄ = (5, 0):

  • ā + b̄ = (−4+5, −3+0) = (1, −3).
  • ā − b̄ = (−4−5, −3−0) = (−9, −3).

8.3.2 Multiplication of a vector by a scalar

Definition: k·AB→ is the vector whose magnitude is k times that of AB→; direction is the same if k > 0, opposite if k < 0.

  • If |k| > 1 it enlarges; if 0 < |k| < 1 it shortens.
  • k(x, y) = (kx, ky).
  • Two vectors are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other: b̄ = k·ā.

Example: ā = (2, 4): −ā = (−2, −4); 2ā = (4, 8); (1/2)ā = (1, 2). All are parallel.

8.4 Position Vector

Definition: Vectors that start at the origin (O) are position vectors.

For AB→ with A=(x₁,y₁), B=(x₂,y₂), the position vector OP→ = P = (x₂−x₁, y₂−y₁) = (x, y).

Notation: OP→ = ū = (x, y) = xi + yj, where i = (1,0) and j = (0,1) are unit vectors in the x and y directions. x and y are the components of ū.

Magnitude: |ū| = √(x² + y²).

Position vector

Example: Position vector ū = (3, 4): starts at origin to (3,4) = 3i + 4j. |ū| = √(9+16) = 5. tan θ = 4/3 → θ ≈ 53°.

Example: Initial (1,3), terminal (2,2) → position vector (2−1, 2−3) = (1, −1).

Example: Initial (−1,−2), terminal (3,1) → (3+1, 1+2) = (4, 3).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Position vector = (x₂−x₁, y₂−y₁). Magnitude |ū| = √(x²+y²). Direction from tan θ = y/x.

8.5 Applications of Vectors in Two Dimensions

Example 1 (displacement): A boat moves 8 km South then 8 km West. Resultant displacement AC = √(8²+8²) = 8√2 km, in direction S 45° W.

Example 2 (rectangle midpoints): ABCD rectangle, E, F, G, H are midpoints. If AE→ = a and AH→ = b, then AF→ = 2a + b, BD→ = 2b − 2a, EC→ = a − 2b. Since BD→ = 2(b−a) = 2 EH→, BD→ is parallel to EH→.

Example 3 (forces): Two perpendicular forces 10 N and 10√3 N. Resultant |R| = √(10² + (10√3)²) = √(100+300) = √400 = 20 N. The third force that counteracts them is 20 N in the opposite direction.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: For perpendicular vectors, resultant |R| = √(|F₁|² + |F₂|²). Use triangle/parallelogram law for non-perpendicular ones.

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 8)

  • Scalar = magnitude only; vector = magnitude + direction.
  • Column vector (x, y); |ā| = √(x²+y²).
  • Equal vectors: same magnitude & direction. Opposite: −ā.
  • Parallel: one is a scalar multiple of the other.
  • Triangle law AB + BC = AC; Parallelogram law (diagonal = sum).
  • Subtract: a − b = a + (−b).
  • k(x,y) = (kx, ky); k>0 same direction, k<0 opposite.
  • Position vector = (x₂−x₁, y₂−y₁) = xi + yj.

UNIT 9: STATISTICS AND PROBABILITY

Note: Based on the official FDRE MoE Grade 9 Mathematics Student Textbook (New Curriculum, 2023), Unit 9.

9.1 Statistical Data

Definition: Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, presenting, analyzing, and interpreting data so that one can make a generalization.

9.1.1 Collection and tabulation of statistical data

Data collection: gathering information from all relevant sources to answer a research problem.

Types of data:

  • Qualitative data — non-numerical characteristics (colour, sex, religion, town).
  • Quantitative data — numerical (scores, heights, weights, ages).
  • Continuous data — measured at any value along a scale (height, temperature, time).
  • Discrete data — counted (usually integers, e.g., number of children; shoe sizes can be halves).

Data collection methods: primary data, secondary data, interviews, direct observations, questionnaires, surveys.

  • Primary data — generated by the researcher (surveys, interviews, experiments).
  • Secondary data — used from data generated by large institutions (government, health facilities).
  • Interview — in-depth (individual) or focus group.
  • Direct observation — systematically selecting, watching, listening, recording behaviour.

Organization: tabulation — condensing data into a statistical table (rows/columns).

Presentation: bar graphs, histograms, pie charts, pictograms, frequency polygons.

Analysis: using mean, median, mode (central tendency) and dispersion.

Interpretation: drawing conclusions about a population from a sample.

Population and sampling

  • Population: the complete collection of individuals, objects, or measurements with a common characteristic.
  • Census: an enumeration of a population (expensive, done every 5–10 years).
  • Sampling frame: the actual set of units from which a sample is drawn.
  • Sample: a small part of the population examined (since the whole is unmanageable, expensive, or destructive).

Example: Study of primary-school study time → population = all primary students; sample = 1,000 selected students.

9.1.2 Graphical presentation of statistical data

  • Frequency distribution table: lists each value (variable) and its frequency (how many times it occurs).
  • Grouped frequency distribution: data grouped into class intervals.
  • Variable: a characteristic that can be measured/observed and varies.
Bar chart
Pie chart

Pie chart: a circle divided into sectors; sector size proportional to frequency. E.g., 120 children: 50% white = 60, 30% purple = 36, 20% blue = 24.

Histogram: graphical representation of a frequency distribution — variable (V) on the x-axis, frequency (f) on the y-axis. Bars touch (no gaps) for continuous data.

Histogram

Example (frequency table): Weights 55, 62, 49, 67, 55, 62, 62, 49, 67, 62, 55, 49 →

Weight (kg)49556267
Frequency3342

Grouped example (ages of 20 customers): classes 0≤x<10 (2), 10≤x<20 (3), 20≤x<30 (3), 30≤x<40 (6), 40≤x<50 (3), 50≤x<60 (1), 60≤x<70 (2).

9.1.3 Measures of central tendency

Mean (average): x̄ = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ)/n = Σx/n. From a frequency distribution: x̄ = Σfx / Σf.

Examples:

  • Textbooks 5,4,6,4,3,6,7 → x̄ = 35/7 = 5.
  • Test scores (freq): x̄ = (10(0)+20(4)+30(1)+40(3)+50(2))/10 = 330/10 = 33.
  • Pencils 6,5,6,5,3,6,6,10,10,3: freq 3(2),5(2),6(4),10(2) → x̄ = (6+10+24+20)/10 = 60/10 = 6.

Properties of the mean:

  1. Sum of deviations from the mean = 0: Σ(x−x̄) = 0.
  2. Adding p to each value → new mean = x̄ + p.
  3. Subtracting p → new mean = x̄ − p.
  4. Multiplying each by p → new mean = p·x̄.
  5. Dividing each by p → new mean = x̄/p.

Median: the middle value of ordered data.

  • Odd number of values: the middle value.
  • Even number: the average of the two middle values.

Example: 65,55,89,56,35,14,56,55,87,45,92 → sorted 14,35,45,55,55,56,56,65,87,89,92 → median = 56 (the 6th of 11).

  • Even example: 14,35,45,55,55,56,56,65,87,89 → median = (55+56)/2 = 55.5.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: ALWAYS sort data before finding the median. For even n, average the two middle values.

Mode: the most frequent value.

  • Example: 5,10,20,20,30,35,35,35,40,50,70,70 → mode = 35.
  • Example (midterm scores): most frequent are 14 and 12 → two modes.
  • If no value repeats (1,3,6,7,9,8,10,17,18) → no mode.
  • The mode is not always unique; it can be used for qualitative data.

9.1.4 Measures of dispersion

Dispersion/variation is the scatter (spread) of data from a measure of central tendency.

Range: Range = Largest value − Smallest value.

Examples:

  • Scores 6,7,5,8,3,8,9,5,4,5.5 → range = 9 − 3 = 6.
  • Freq table values 1,2,4,5,6 → range = 6 − 1 = 5.

Variance: the mean of the squared deviations from the mean: σ² = Σ(x−x̄)² / n.

Standard deviation: the square root of the variance: σ = √σ² = √(Σ(x−x̄)²/n).

Steps: find mean → deviations (x−x̄) → square them → average (variance) → square root (σ).

Example (TVs sold): 13,8,4,9,7,12,10 → x̄ = 63/7 = 9. Deviations²: 16,1,25,0,4,9,1 → σ² = 56/7 = 8, σ = √8 ≈ 2.83.

Grouped example (hours watching TV, 48 students): x̄ = 432/48 = 9; Σf(x−x̄)² = 124 → σ² = 124/48 = 31/12 ≈ 2.58, σ ≈ 1.6.

Properties of variance/standard deviation:

  1. Adding a constant k to each value → variance and σ unchanged.
  2. Multiplying each value by c → new variance = c²·(old); new σ = |c|·(old).

Example: data 2,3,4,3: x̄ = 3; deviations −1,0,1,0; σ² = (1+0+1+0)/4 = 0.5; σ ≈ 0.707. Adding 3 → 5,6,7,6 → new x̄ = 6; σ² still 0.5, σ still 0.707.

9.2 Probability

Definition: Probability is a numerical value that describes the likelihood of the occurrence of an event in an experiment.

Experimental probability is determined from data collected by repeating an experiment.

  • Experiment: a trial by which an observation is obtained but whose outcome cannot be predicted in advance.
  • Equally likely outcomes: each outcome occurs equally often when repeated many times.
  • Definition: If an experiment has n equally likely outcomes and m is a particular outcome, then probability = m/n.

Example (tossing a coin twice): possible outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT.

  • Probability of exactly one tail = 2/4 = 1/2 (HT, TH).
  • Probability of at least one head = 3/4 (HH, HT, TH).

Sample space and event

  • Sample space (S): the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
  • Event: a subset of the sample space.

Examples:

  • Toss one coin: S = {H, T}.
  • Throw one die: S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}.
  • Toss two coins: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}.

Example (cards): Numbers 4 to 30 on cards, choose one at random. S = {4,5,…,30}. Events: "number divisible by 3" = {6,9,12,…,30}; "number even" = {4,6,8,…,30}.

Probability of an event

Definition: The theoretical probability of event E: P(E) = n(E)/n(S) = (favourable outcomes)/(total outcomes).

Example (die): P(odd) = P({1,3,5}) = 3/6 = 1/2.

Example (workers): 45 men, 55 women out of 100 → P(man) = 45/100 = 0.45.

Example (coin + die): tree diagram gives 12 outcomes. P(tail and odd) = 3/12 = 1/4. P(head and number ≤ 5) = 5/12.

Experimental vs theoretical: Toss a coin 10,000 times, get 5,010 heads. Tails = 4,990 → P(tails) = 4990/10000 = 0.499 (close to 1/2).

Tree diagrams

Used when many combined events are considered. Each branch shows a possible outcome and its probability.

Tree diagram for coin tosses

Example (three coins): S = {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT} (8 outcomes).

  • P(exactly two heads) = 3/8.
  • P(exactly one tail) = 3/8.
  • P(three tails) = 1/8.
  • P(at least two heads) = 4/8 = 1/2.

Example (coin + die): 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes. P(head and even) = 3/12 = 1/4.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: P(E) = n(E)/n(S). Sample space = all outcomes; event = subset. Use tree diagrams to count combined-outcome probabilities.

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 9)

  • Statistics = collecting, organizing, presenting, analyzing, interpreting data.
  • Qualitative vs quantitative; continuous vs discrete.
  • Primary vs secondary data.
  • Population (whole) vs sample (subset); census.
  • Frequency distribution table; histogram (V on x, f on y).
  • Mean x̄ = Σx/n = Σfx/Σf; properties of mean.
  • Median = middle of ordered data (avg of two middles for even n).
  • Mode = most frequent (may be non-unique or absent).
  • Range = max − min.
  • Variance σ² = Σ(x−x̄)²/n; σ = √variance.
  • Adding constant: variance unchanged; multiplying by c: variance × c², σ × |c|.
  • Probability P(E) = n(E)/n(S).
  • Sample space, event, equally likely, tree diagrams.
